R2 (no dominant method) resolved NR-243's four red pairs WITHOUT changing any recipe magnitude: measured against the axis scripts/recipes.lua already states in its own comments, three pairs have disjoint raws (supply routes, where deposit access rather than price decides) and the fourth differs by a placement precondition, so all four were artefacts of grouping by (primary output, era). Every sibling pair is now bucketed as supply route / precondition / genuine interchangeable method, and only the third is price-compared; the duplicate guard in recipe_switch_harness was deleted rather than left as a second answer, and that harness now runs ALL PASS. Current reading: 4 sibling pairs — 3 supply routes, 1 precondition, 0 interchangeable methods, so the dominance half guards an empty set until BL-430's own alternates are authored (NR-258). Two measurement traps found and closed while building: era_band::industrial is a band like any other and masks the whole ancient roster (misreported charcoal/iron_blooms/timber/clay/peat as orphans, hid two of the four sibling pairs) — both rows use era_band::any; and endemic goods reach the world via planetology::endemics in tile_generation.cpp, NOT via k_extractable, so without that second obtainability route all four endemics read as orphans.
items.title: One harness for the roster invariants — no orphan resources, no unplaceable buildings, no dominant method, no cyclic graph
items.summary: The saved check for the economy-breadth sprint, filed as its own item so it is built rather than promised. Four invariants over the loaded registry: the recipe graph is acyclic (or depth is undefined), every resource_type in the enum has a producer or a consumer (BL-340's admission rule, mechanised), every building's declared minimum depth is reachable from a fresh start, and no production method dominates a sibling on every axis (BL-430's design bar).
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-15 with the economy-breadth sprint, under CLAUDE.md § "Tool creation is skill
creation" - a roster this size will not stay coherent by authorship alone, and the check
written now catches next quarter's orphan.

## Why a harness and not a review pass

BL-286 is the cautionary precedent and it is in the code comments: eleven resource values were
added with "behaviour unfiled", and five of them still have no consumer today, months later.
No human reading a diff catches that; a load-time graph walk catches it in a second. The same
goes for a building nobody can place and a method nobody would ever pick.

## The four assertions

1. **Acyclic.** Depth (BL-428) is undefined on a cycle. Fail loudly at load rather than loop.
2. **No orphans, both directions.** Every `resource_type` is produced by some recipe or
   extractable from some deposit, AND consumed by some recipe or bought by some named actor.
   Terminal goods declare themselves terminal so they are exempt from the second half - an
   explicit exemption list, so an orphan cannot hide as an assumed terminal.
3. **Every building reachable.** For each building's minimum depth, a path exists from a fresh
   corp's starting position to that depth. An unplaceable building is the roster's orphan.
4. **No dominant method.** For each output with alternates, no sibling is better on every axis
   (input cost at reference prices, wage, rate, depth). This is BL-430's design bar mechanised.

## Determinism note

The walk must not depend on container iteration order - the BL-406 lesson, where an unordered
container decided a number the economy read. Sort by authored recipe id before walking, and
assert the depth vector is byte-identical across two loads in the same process.

Runs as `tools/verify/chain_depth.cpp` under the `verifier-headless` skill, named in the skill
so it is discoverable, and added to the ctest tier.

items.title: Let the player choose their starting corporation, instead of being assigned one by the seed
items.summary: Measured 2026-08-16: 13 of 24 seeds hand the player a pure-extraction corp with no processing facility, so the Method page and the chain-depth ladder have nothing to work with — while every one of those same worlds contains other corporations that do have processors. Solvency is not the problem (all 24 seeds end positive, none dip). The fix is to stop assigning the player a corp by lottery and let them choose from the world's own corporations, which is the deferred corporation selection screen CORPORATION_GENERATION.md already names.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-16, from a live look at an autostarted campaign whose player corp
held no processing facility at all — so the Method page (BL-430/BL-431's whole
surface) had nothing to show, and the chain-depth ladder (BL-428) had no rung to
stand on.

## The measurement that prompted it

`tools/verify/player_seed_sweep.cpp` (written the same session) over 24 seeds,
12 warm ticks:

  * 11/24 hand the player a corp with at least one processing facility.
  * 13/24 give a PURE-EXTRACTION corp — no processing at all.
  * 3 of those (seeds 9, 12, 22) give no production building of any kind.
  * Solvency is NOT the discriminator: every one of the 24 seeds ends positive
    (1.3k - 55k cr) and not one dips below zero on the way.

That last line matters, because the instinct was to filter on profitability. The
economy is not producing broke openings; it is producing SHALLOW ones.

## Why a selection screen rather than a seed filter

The obvious fix — reject seeds whose player corp lacks a processor — is a hidden
constraint that makes the world generator quietly lie about its own distribution,
and it throws away half the seeds to fix a problem that is really about WHICH corp
in the world the player is handed. Every one of those 13 worlds contains plenty of
corporations with processing facilities; the player was simply assigned a poor one.

`docs/generation/CORPORATION_GENERATION.md` already carries the deferred
"corporation selection screen" as an open item. This is that item, now with a
measured reason to exist: it converts an invisible seed lottery into a stated
choice, and it is the honest version of the fix (the player sees the opening
positions and picks, rather than the generator silently discarding worlds).

## Shape

1. After generation, present the campaign's corporations as selectable openings —
   name, home nation, industrial focus, starting assets by type, opening balance.
2. The player picks; `world::player_entity` is set from the choice rather than by
   the generator's own assignment.
3. A "surprise me" option keeps the current behaviour for players who want it.
4. The New World wizard (docs/ui/STARTUP.md) is the natural host — a stage between
   generation completing and Begin.

## Interaction with the sweep

`player_seed_sweep` stays a REPORTING tool either way: once selection exists, its
"no processing facility" column stops being a rejection reason and becomes a
description of one candidate among several. Worth keeping as the guard that the
generator still produces a spread of openings worth choosing between.

## Deliberately not doing

Rejection-sampling seeds at generation time, or shipping a hard-coded whitelist of
"good" seeds. Both hide the distribution rather than exposing it, and the second
would rot the moment generation changes.
items.progress: COMPLETE 2026-08-17, 6 of 6 tasks. A-D landed 2026-08-16 (see below). E and F landed on resume. (E) The screen was unreachable to --verify - both automated paths take the Surprise-me fallback by design, which is what keeps every other capture bit-identical - so E built the hook first: verify.show_corp_choice re-enters the stage from a started world, verify.corp_choices() exposes the armed list, and scripts/verify/corp_choice.lua asserts (a choice exists, the pool is specialist-sized, every row named and focused) then captures. It caught a real defect on its first run: the Holdings cell clipped to "/ 1 otl" behind the Choose button, fixed by rebalancing the column weights. Headless half: player_seed_sweep --guard, G1-G4 over 24 seeds ALL PASS (8 specialists/seed, 166 of 192 with a processor = 6.92/8 against a 4.00 floor and a 2.96 pre-BL-435 baseline, 0 dead, 0 mis-flagged), registered as its own ctest at 12 seeds. build_corp_choices also now skips is_background explicitly, so the specialist-only pool stops being a property of WHEN it runs. (F) Propagated to CORPORATION_GENERATION.md (the deferred selection screen it named is described as built, with the still-deferred half stated honestly - the analytical profile and the re-roll verbs), STARTUP.md (five-state machine + a stage section) and question_log.json. Carried into every doc: this is a DEPTH choice, not a wealth one - BL-436 measured processing as earning less than the extraction it replaces, so nothing claims the processor-bearing corp is richer. OWED: Ben has still not eyeballed the layout, so corp_choice is capture-only with NO golden (NR-275). Review entries filed: NR-273, NR-274, NR-275.
items.dead_start_fix:
DEAD-START FIX 2026-08-16, from Ben during the Sprint 19 playtest: 'the main problem we still have to solve is the extreme difference in viability between different starts. We shouldn't be seeding such corporations as the default one, which has no way of making money at all.'

ROOT CAUSE, and it was a call made earlier the same session. holdings_range gave TRADE corps 1-2 holdings against focus_asset_pattern's trade mix, whose FIRST slot is a port. A 1-draw therefore opened a corporation holding nothing but a port - and port carries base_rate 0, so it produces nothing. That corp had no income source whatsoever: not a lean opening, a dead one. When the processor question was settled earlier this session, trade was deliberately left without a processor as 'a real archetype'. An archetype with no income is not one, and that reasoning did not check whether a trade corp could earn AT ALL.

It reached the PLAYER on 3 of 24 seeds (9, 12, 22 - all reading '0 proc, 0 extr').

FIX: trade holdings_range 1-2 -> 2-3, which guarantees the trade pattern's second slot (an extraction site). Every trade corp can now earn from tick one. The 3-draw additionally reaches the pattern's processing slot, so processor coverage rises as a side effect rather than by design.

MEASURED: dead specialist corps 0 of 192 across 24 seeds (was 3 player-facing plus more among the non-player specialists). Player-corp playability 18/24 -> 21/24; the remaining 3 rejections are 'no processing facility', which is the softer condition selection is for. player_seed_sweep gained a standing CANNOT PRODUCE AT ALL row so a dead start can never be seeded silently again.

Goldens: ai_skill_harness re-blessed - every net worth ROSE and solvency IMPROVED on three seeds (1, 2, 3 now spend zero ticks below zero), which is the fix working rather than drift. spectator_determinism re-blessed for the changed world. world_audit's B4 row needed its hand-mirrored holdings table updated - the THIRD mirrored table to drift out of date in one session, after ai_skill_harness's richness fields and both harnesses' base_rate.

items.title: A processing facility earns less than the extraction site it replaces — the whole refining chain is a net income loss
items.summary: Measured 2026-08-16 while landing BL-435: swapping ONE extraction site for ONE processing facility on the same corp, same seed, halves its balance (55,179 -> 28,288 cr), and the same swap across the generated economy moves ai_skill_harness's five seeds by -71/-37/-9/-20/-38% on final net worth. Refining is supposed to be the value-add step the whole economy is built around; today it is a way to earn less. Filed as its own item on Ben's call so BL-435 is not blocked by an economy rebalance.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call on NR-260, option B), out of BL-435's generation fix.

## The measurement, and why it is trustworthy

This is an unusually clean natural experiment, which is why it is worth acting on
rather than filing as a hunch. BL-435 moved the processor in `focus_asset_pattern`
from a slot the holdings draw rarely reached to one it always reaches. Nothing
else changed: same seeds, same tiles, same corps, same recipes, same prices. The
ONLY difference is that some corps now open with 2 extraction + 1 processing where
they previously opened with 3 extraction + 0 processing.

  * Player corp, seed 0: 55,178.8 -> 28,288.2 cr after 12 warm ticks. Halved.
  * ai_skill_harness final net worth, all five seeds, 30-tick rollouts:
      seed 0  181,559 -> 51,950   (-71%)
      seed 1  110,289 -> 69,804   (-37%)
      seed 2  173,754 -> 157,314  ( -9%)
      seed 3  621,950 -> 500,635  (-20%)
      seed 4  205,193 -> 126,637  (-38%)

Every seed moved the same direction. A single-building swap is not supposed to be
worth 20-70% of an economy.

## Why this is a design problem and not just a number

RESOURCES.md's whole tier model says margin WIDENS up the tiers - Tier 3 promises
the "widest price divergence", and BL-340 priced the chain that way on purpose
(spacecraft_components at 56x iron ore). PRODUCTION.md's processing chain is the
value-add step the trade pillar rests on. If a mine outearns the refinery fed by
it, then:

  * the chain-depth growth track (BL-428) asks the player to climb a ladder that
    costs money at every rung;
  * BL-430's alternate methods are a choice between ways of losing income;
  * BL-435's selection screen would present a corp with a processor as the better
    opening while it is in fact the poorer one;
  * and `corp_ai`'s build scorer is being asked to prefer processors on a payback
    curve that does not reward them (read alongside BL-417, which already flags
    the score as quadratic in net margin).

## What is NOT yet known, and should be measured before tuning

The cause is unidentified and there are at least four candidates. Measure first -
the standing lesson from Sprint 11 and Sprint 18 is that the plausible story loses
to the measurement about half the time:

  1. **Input cost vs output price.** Steel at 8.0 against 2 iron ore (2.5) + 1 coal
     (2.0) = 7.0 is a margin of 1.0 per unit, ~14%. An extraction site sells its
     raw output with no input cost at all. Check the whole recipe table this way -
     `chain_depth`'s R2 row already computes input-basket cost and could report it.
  2. **Wages and maintenance.** BL-049 split these; a processing facility may
     simply carry a heavier fixed cost per unit of output than a mine.
  3. **Market depth.** A processor must BUY its inputs from a market that may not
     carry them, so it idles or runs starved while a mine always has its deposit.
     If so the defect is availability, not price, and the fix is different.
  4. **Throughput.** Rates may differ enough that per-tick output value diverges
     regardless of per-unit margin.

## Done when

A processing facility fed by its own inputs earns MORE than the extraction site it
replaced, over a representative rollout - or there is a written, deliberate reason
why it should not, propagated into PRODUCTION.md. Either outcome closes it; the
current state, where the arrangement is accidental and undocumented, does not.

Guarded by a headless row so it cannot regress silently: the natural home is
`econ_harness` or a new margin-by-tier check, asserting the tier ordering the docs
already promise.
items.measurement:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 by the new tools/verify/tier_margin.cpp (3 seeds x 20 ticks, real generated world, real Lua economy, reading estimate_building_profit - the same per-building breakdown the Profitability page shows a player). Per building-tick, mean:
  extraction_site      revenue 1954.62  input 0.00   maint 5.84  wage 1.28  NET +1947.50  earning 85%
  processing_facility  revenue    4.62  input 14.18  maint 7.53  wage 1.08  NET   -18.18  earning 22%
Extraction out-earns processing ~107x on net, and processing is outright LOSS-MAKING: capex payback is 0 ticks against NEVER.

THE CAUSE IS NOT PRICING, and that rules out the item's first candidate. It is a structural asymmetry in how the two rates are computed (economy_system.cpp):
  extraction: base_rate 20 x RICHNESS x workforce x (1 - hazard)
  processing: base_rate 8 x workforce                     <- no comparable multiplier exists
components.hpp documents resource_deposit as 'deposit richness (the extraction rate multiplier)' and tile_generation rolls it at 20-50, so an extraction site produces on the order of 780 units/tick while a processor makes 8 batches. The revenue gap is 423x; the per-unit recipe margin (steel 8.0 against inputs 7.0, ~14%) is almost irrelevant beside it.

SECOND CAUSE, independent and additive: a processor produces NOTHING on 78% of its building-ticks (earning 22% vs extraction's 85%) while still paying wages and maintenance. That is the item's market-depth candidate confirmed - it cannot buy its inputs - and it means even a rate fix alone would leave most processors idle.

So of the four candidates filed: throughput (4) is the dominant cause but at a STRUCTURAL level rather than a tuning one; market depth (3) is a real and separate contributor; input-cost-vs-price (1) and wages/maintenance (2) are both rounding errors at this magnitude - fixed costs are ~8.6/tick against a 1947/tick gap.
items.starvation_measurement:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: measure the starvation before choosing a rate fix). tier_margin R3 classifies every processing building-tick by the reason the ECONOMY ITSELF recorded in building_report, rather than by inference. Over 3 seeds x 20 ticks, 1279 processing building-ticks:
  produced output           38.9%
  STARVED (input missing)   34.9%
  no recipe set             11.3%
  idle, no reason recorded  14.9%
  unstaffed                  0.0%

So 'processors do nothing 78% of the time' decomposes into THREE independent problems, not one, and only the first is the market-depth cause the item guessed:
  1. STARVATION, 34.9% - the largest. Binding input when starved is dominated by COAL (resource id 1) at 38.5% of starved ticks, far ahead of silica 11.6%, rare_earth_ore 10.7% and ree_alloy 10.7%. Coal is a raw with deposits and a price; it is the steel recipe's reagent, and steel is the era-aware DEFAULT recipe, so most processors want coal and cannot get it. Worth checking whether anything actually mines coal at scale before assuming a market-routing fault.
  2. NO RECIPE SET, 11.3% - a straight defect, and these buildings can never produce while still paying wages and maintenance. app::load_economy assigns a default to every unconfigured processor, but it runs BEFORE generate_background_firms, so processors created by the background-firm pass that its own gap-relief chooser did not assign a recipe to are left at no_recipe permanently. Likely a cheap fix with a disproportionate effect.
  3. IDLE, NO REASON RECORDED, 14.9% - unexplained. Not starved, not unstaffed, has a recipe. Needs its own look; the report has no field that explains these.

METHOD NOTE, because it inverted the answer once. Measuring WITHOUT load_economy's default-recipe pass reports no-recipe at 26.5% and starvation at 20.9% - i.e. it reverses which cause is largest. That pass is a real startup stage, not a harness convenience (recipe ids are registry indices that do not exist at generation time), and it runs before background firms. tier_margin now performs it by default and documents why; the opt-out remains only to isolate how much the pass is carrying.
items.rate_fix_progress:
RATE ASYMMETRY FIXED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call). Framed as a RESTORATION, not a rebalance: building_economics::base_rate has always documented itself as 'units/tick AT RICHNESS 1', while tile_component::resource_deposit is generated as a QUANTITY (measured mean 53.3, max 72,321) and was multiplied in raw. Mine effective rate ~1067 against a processor's flat 8 - a 133:1 structural gap (tier_margin R6).

Richness is now divided by a measured reference and clamped to a band, all three authored in scripts/economy.lua (richness_reference 53.3, min 0.25, max 2.0). A reference of 0 disables the conversion and restores raw behaviour, so an un-migrated economy.lua is unchanged. The design statement behind the clamp: richness decides how LONG a deposit lasts, not how fast you can pull it out - reserve still scales with raw richness, so a rich tile is still worth far more over its life.

Applied at ALL FOUR sites that compute a rate from richness, via one shared free function (richness_rate_scalar) so a preview cannot drift from the tick: extraction_nominal (the live tick), the BL-181 workforce solver, building_profit's expected-output estimate (shown on the Build door), and corp_ai's build-candidate revenue estimate (which gates on net <= 0, so a raw richness had the scorer expecting ~50x the revenue a site delivers).

RESULT: extraction revenue 1942.80 -> 11.07/tick, net 1935.85 -> 4.75, capex payback 0 ticks -> 21. Extraction is a real business rather than a money fountain, and the two tiers are finally the same order of magnitude. Processing is still -19.95/tick, so R2 still FAILS - but what remains is a genuine balance question at comparable scale rather than a structural absurdity, which is what this step was for.

CRITICAL CAVEAT ON THE GREEN SUITE, and it must not be read as safety: ai_skill_harness and spectator_determinism both PASSED unchanged, and that is because they HAND-BUILD their recipe registry and never load scripts/economy.lua. richness_reference therefore defaults to 0.0 in both, the conversion is disabled, and they measured the OLD rate model. Their goldens are vacuous with respect to this change - exactly the hand-built-fixture trap the verifier-headless skill documents (BL-404 is the precedent). The AI's real behaviour under the new rates is UNMEASURED.
items.harness_gap_closed:
HARNESS GAP CLOSED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: close it before playtesting), AND IT IMMEDIATELY FOUND WHAT IT WAS HIDING.

ai_skill_harness and spectator_determinism hand-build a recipe_registry that CLAIMS to mirror scripts/economy.lua. It had fallen out of date: neither set richness_reference, so it defaulted to 0, the BL-436 conversion was disabled, and both harnesses measured the PRE-BL-436 rate model while reporting ALL PASS. The three fields are now mirrored in both, with a comment saying why leaving them unset is not a harmless omission.

WITH THE MIRROR RESTORED, THE AI ECONOMY COLLAPSES. Final net worth across the five benchmark seeds, previously all positive:
  seed 0  +51,950 -> -22,787   solvency 10/30 -> 18/30 below zero, survival 0.86 -> 0.71
  seed 1  +69,804 ->  -8,282   solvency  0/30 -> 12/30,             survival 0.86 -> 0.43
  seed 2 +157,314 -> -56,070   solvency  5/30 -> 20/30,             survival 1.00
  seed 3 +500,635 -> -75,806   solvency  0/30 -> 24/30,             survival 0.71
  seed 4 +126,637 ->  -6,194   solvency  7/30 -> 11/30,             survival 0.57
17 assertions fail. Every rival corporation goes insolvent.

WHAT THIS MEANS. The rate fix is directionally right - it removed a 133:1 structural absurdity - but the CALIBRATION is wrong, and the reason is now obvious in hindsight: the entire cost side of the economy (maintenance 5, wage 8, build_cost 100, starting capital) was tuned against extraction earning ~1947/tick, where costs were effectively free. Cutting extraction income ~410x to 4.75/tick leaves costs dominating everything, so no corp can fund its own operation.

The band cannot fix this on its own: with richness_max 2.0 the best possible site earns ~22/tick revenue, so raising the reference or widening the band only moves a ceiling that is already far below the cost base. The levers that actually reach it are extraction base_rate, the maintenance/wage/build_cost scale, or starting capital - i.e. a deliberate re-tune of the cost side to match the corrected income side. THAT IS A DESIGN DECISION AND IS BEN'S; nothing is being tuned on his behalf.

GOLDENS DELIBERATELY NOT RE-BLESSED. Blessing a set of numbers in which every AI corporation is bankrupt would record economic collapse as the expected state. They stay red until the calibration is settled.

This is the whole argument for closing a harness gap before playtesting: the previous run of this same harness reported ALL PASS on exactly this code.
items.calibration_sweep:
CALIBRATION ATTEMPTED AND NOT SETTLED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: settle it before playtesting). The conversion is LANDED BUT DISABLED - scripts/economy.lua sets richness_reference = 0.0, which is the documented off switch; set it to 53.3 to enable. Everything else about the fix is in place.

THE SWEEP. Hypothesis: normalising richness fixed the 133:1 RATIO but also cut absolute SCALE ~53x, and the cost side (maintenance 5, wage 8, build_cost 100, starting capital) was tuned against the old inflated income - so restore scale by multiplying BOTH producer base_rates together, holding the 2.5:1 ratio. Measured at three points (tier_margin, per building-tick):

  scale   extraction net   processing net   processing earning%   AI net worth (5 seeds)
  x1      +4.75            -19.95           18%                   all 5 bankrupt, -6k to -76k
  x4      +27.95           -61.86            4%                   4 of 5 bankrupt, to -250k
  x10     +75.25           -58.16            4%                   (not run; x4 already worse)

THE HYPOTHESIS IS WRONG AND THE SWEEP KILLED IT. Scale is not the lever. Raising extraction income makes the collapse WORSE, not better, because corps spend the extra income building processors that lose MORE per tick at higher scale - and processing's 'earning' share FALLS from 18% to 4% as scale rises, because scaling multiplies a processor's input demand against a supply that does not scale with it. Seeds 1 and 3 reach -225k and -250k at x4 against -8k and -76k at x1.

WHAT THAT LEAVES. The AI collapse is driven by PROCESSING LOSSES, not by extraction income, so the calibration cannot be settled by any number on the extraction side. The open half of BL-436 is therefore processing profitability itself, and it has two identified components already measured: (a) starvation - processors earn on 18% of ticks at best, and BL-437's co-extraction only lifted coal to ~98 units/tick against roughly 5x that in demand; (b) the per-batch margin against fixed costs - steel clears 1.0/batch at 8 batches/tick = 8 gross against 22 in maintenance + wages, so steel processing loses ~14/tick EVEN AT 100% UPTIME. (b) is arithmetic and can be settled without a sweep; (a) needs supply work.

LEFT DISABLED RATHER THAN HALF-TUNED so the tree is green and playable: with the conversion off, ai_skill_harness and every other golden pass unchanged. tier_margin still fails R2 and R4 by design - those two rows ARE the open work.
items.harness_price_gap:
MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT WAS WRONG, CORRECTED 2026-08-16. Going after the processing margin, R7 (authored base_price vs live market price) showed only 14 resources priced in any market - COAL among the missing - which read as 'processors starve because coal has no market'. That was the HARNESS, not the game: tier_margin loaded recipes.lua and economy.lua but NOT world_gen.lua, which carries the market base_price table, so markets fell back to world_gen_config.hpp's built-in defaults. This is exactly BL-389's defect (--serve never loads world_gen.lua either), reproduced by omission in a brand-new harness written to diagnose the economy. A harness that loads two of the three economy scripts measures an economy the game never runs. Fixed: world_gen.lua is loaded and world_gen_config.cpp linked; 36 resources now price.

THE CORRECTED NUMBERS MOVE MATERIALLY, so earlier figures on this item should be read as suspect wherever they involve prices or input cost:
                       broken harness   corrected
  processing net       -19.95           -9.32
  processing earning    18%              50%
  starved               34.9%            30.1%
  no recipe set         11.1%             9.4%

WHAT THE CORRECTED MEASUREMENT SAYS. Processing revenue 12.84 against input cost 13.15 - a GROSS margin of about -0.31 per building-tick, i.e. the recipes are roughly value-NEUTRAL at live prices before a single fixed cost. Maintenance 7.85 and wages 1.16 then carry it to -9.32. So both halves are real and neither alone explains it: the chain adds no value at market prices, AND fixed costs are unfunded. Note this is measured with the richness conversion DISABLED (the calibration is still open), so extraction still reads 1695/tick.

NOT FIXED. The margin work stopped here deliberately rather than tuning on top of numbers that had just moved under it.

items.title: Eight raw resources with deposits are mined by NOTHING - a site takes only the richest deposit on its tile, and iron ore always wins
items.summary: Measured 2026-08-16 by tier_margin R4 while chasing BL-436. Coal sits on 1671 tiles with ZERO extraction sites; so do rare_earth_ore (10373 tiles), regolith (16361), peat (4358), clay (2146), sand (1601), iron_nickel_ore (330) and platinum_group_metals (117). Iron ore gets 44 sites and 75,478 units/tick - more than every other resource combined by two orders of magnitude. Cause: placement_rules::richest_extractable gives a site the single richest deposit on its tile, so a resource never richest anywhere is never mined, however many tiles carry it and however badly a recipe needs it. [COMPLETE 2026-08-16, flipped 2026-08-19 by the N1 audit: 2884f6c — option B, a site works EVERY deposit on its tile with shared capacity (economy_system.cpp:116,:192-209); full harness suite passed per the item record; unproduced inputs 8→3, residue = R5 group-1 off-world raws, out of scope. Caveat recorded honestly: no requirements group was ever written for this item, so the evidence is the item prose + harness list, not a row-by-row gate.]
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 out of BL-436's measurement chain. BL-436 asked why refining does not pay; R3 said processors starve; R4 asked what they starve ON, and the answer is much larger than the question.

## The measurement (tier_margin R4, 3 seeds x 20 ticks, real generated world)

  id  resource                tiles   sites   units/tick
   0  iron_ore                55466      44     75478.3
   6  agricultural_produce    12315      30      5047.3
   7  water                   14042       5      1556.0
   3  silica                  21881      10       557.9
   2  petroleum                2756       2       515.0
  12  timber                   5404      11       385.1
   4  copper_ore              17445       3       305.6
  11  stone                   83461       8       164.5
   1  coal                     1671       0         0.0   <-- MINED BY NOTHING
   5  rare_earth_ore          10373       0         0.0   <--
   8  iron_nickel_ore           330       0         0.0   <--
   9  platinum_group_metals     117       0         0.0   <--
  10  regolith                16361       0         0.0   <--
  13  sand                     1601       0         0.0   <--
  14  clay                     2146       0         0.0   <--
  15  peat                     4358       0         0.0   <--

Eight of the sixteen mineable raws are produced in ZERO quantity, and every one is named as an input by at least one authored recipe. Iron ore alone out-produces everything else combined by two orders of magnitude.

## The cause, and it is one function

placement_rules::richest_extractable walks k_extractable and returns the resource with the highest resource_deposit value on that tile. One tile, one resource, winner takes all. Iron ore is on 55,466 tiles - more than any raw except stone - so on almost any tile worth siting a mine on, iron ore is the pick. A resource that is never the richest on any tile is unreachable by construction. The deposits are there in quantity; the SELECTION rule is what excludes them.

## Why priority A: it is upstream of several filed problems

  * BL-436 (processing does not pay): `steel` is the era-aware DEFAULT recipe and needs coal as its reagent. Nothing mines coal, so the default recipe can NEVER run - most of the 34.9% starvation R3 measured, with coal alone at 38.5% of all starved ticks.
  * BL-428's chain depth asks the player to climb a graph whose lower rungs cannot be supplied.
  * BL-429/BL-430's ancient roster consumes peat, clay and sand - all three unmined - so a large part of that content is unreachable in play.
  * BL-435's selection screen presents corps with processors as richer openings when those processors may have no possible input.

## Options, none costed

  A) A site targets a resource CHOSEN AT PLACEMENT (by the builder, or by what the local market lacks) rather than by richest-deposit. Most faithful to the design - a mine is sited FOR something - and it makes the Build door a real decision. Largest change: corp_ai, corporation_generation and the player build path all pick targets via richest_extractable today.
  B) One site works SEVERAL deposits on its tile, so a tile's coal is reachable alongside its iron. Smallest code change; weakens the tile-choice decision.
  C) Bias richest_extractable by scarcity or unmet demand rather than raw richness. Cheapest, but a heuristic patch on a rule whose problem is that it is a heuristic.

MEASURE BEFORE CHOOSING (BL-436's own lesson): check whether the eight are never the richest ANYWHERE, or merely never on the tiles corps actually site on. Different problems - B only fixes the second.

## Guarded by

tier_margin R4's assertion - 'every recipe input that has deposits is mined by at least one site' - fails today naming the count (8), and passes when this lands.
items.measurement_r5:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: run the never-richest-anywhere measurement before costing any option). tier_margin R5 reports, per resource, the share of tiles carrying it on which it is the RICHEST - i.e. how often richest_extractable would actually return it. Computed with the real function, not a reimplementation.

  id  resource                tiles  richest   win%  sites
  10  regolith                16361    15644  95.6%      0
   8  iron_nickel_ore           330      220  66.7%      0
   5  rare_earth_ore          10373     1273  12.3%      0
  15  peat                     4358       56   1.3%      0
   1  coal                     1671       19   1.1%      0
   9  platinum_group_metals     117        1   0.9%      0
  13  sand                     1601        2   0.1%      0
  14  clay                     2146        0   0.0%      0
  (for contrast: water 100%, silica 74.5%, agri 70.0%, iron_ore 38.6% - all mined)

THIS CORRECTS THIS ITEM AS FILED. The filing treated all eight as one problem caused by one rule. They are THREE problems:

  1. OFF-WORLD REACH, not the rule: regolith (95.6% win) and iron_nickel_ore (66.7%) are the richest almost everywhere they occur and still have zero sites. The rule would happily return them; nothing mines them because no corp operates on airless bodies or metallic asteroids in Era 0. That is the era gate working as designed and is NOT in this item's scope. Two of the eight are therefore expected, and the headline 'eight raws mined by nothing' overstated the defect.
  2. OUT-RANKED IN PRACTICE, and this is the real item: coal 1.1%, rare_earth_ore 12.3%, peat 1.3%, sand 0.1%, PGM 0.9%. They are present on thousands of tiles but something outranks them almost everywhere, so in practice richest_extractable never returns them. 'Never richest anywhere' turned out to be the wrong question - the win RATE is what matters, and a binary richest-somewhere/never test would have given a confidently wrong answer for coal.
  3. NEVER RICHEST: clay alone, at 0.0%.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE OPTIONS. Option B (one site works several deposits on its tile) now looks much stronger than when filed: groups 2 and 3 are precisely the case where the resource COEXISTS with a richer one on the same tile, so working several deposits reaches all of them - coal, sand, peat, clay and rare_earth in one change. It does nothing for group 1, but group 1 does not need it. Option A remains the most faithful to the design and is still the larger change. Option C is now the weakest: biasing the winner still picks exactly one resource per tile, so it would unblock coal only by starving whatever it displaced.

THE COAL CASE IS THE URGENT ONE regardless of which option wins: `steel` is the era-aware default recipe, coal is its reagent, and coal is mined nowhere - so the DEFAULT recipe can never run in a shipped campaign. That single fact is most of BL-436's starvation.
items.progress:
OPTION B BUILT 2026-08-16 (Ben's call). run_extraction now works EVERY deposit on the site's tile, sharing the site's unchanged capacity across them in proportion to richness. target_resource survives as the PRIMARY - it still sets the rate, the stack key and the taper, and still names the site for UI and AI - but a mine now yields a BASKET.

CAPACITY IS SHARED, NOT MULTIPLIED, and that was the load-bearing decision: yielding every deposit at full rate would have multiplied extraction output several-fold, widening the very gap BL-436 exists to close. Measured extraction net held at 1935.85/tick against 1947.50 before - a 0.6% drop, i.e. no inflation.

RESULT, exactly as R5 predicted:
  coal            0.0 -> 98.2 units/tick
  rare_earth_ore  0.0 -> 518.8
  sand            0.0 -> 139.6
  clay            0.0 -> 129.3
  peat            0.0 -> 123.1
  (also up: stone 164.5 -> 2876.9, silica 557.9 -> 2704.9, copper_ore 305.6 -> 987.4)
  (iron_ore 75145 -> 69609, the sharing showing up as intended)
Unproduced inputs fell 8 -> 3. The remaining three are iron_nickel_ore, platinum_group_metals and regolith - R5's group 1, unmined because no corp operates off-world in Era 0. This fix neither addresses nor should address them.

WHAT IT DID NOT FIX, stated plainly: processing is still loss-making at -18.21/tick, and starvation barely moved (34.9% -> 33.4% of processing building-ticks). Coal now flows but at ~98 units/tick against a demand of roughly 8 coal per processor-tick across ~65 processors - still about 5x short, because coal's share of a tile's richness is small precisely where it is rarely the richest. So option B removed the ABSOLUTE blocker (a default recipe whose reagent nothing produced) without closing BL-436. The rate asymmetry remains the dominant cause and is untouched.

HARNESS BUG FOUND AND FIXED IN THE SAME PASS: tier_margin R4 attributed a site's whole output to its primary target_resource, so on the first post-fix run it reported coal as MINED BY NOTHING while coal was coming out of the ground. Supply is now measured as RESERVE DEPLETION, which nothing but extraction moves, and the assertion is keyed on production rather than on how many sites name a resource as their primary.

Verified: econ_harness, econ_stability, econ_bankruptcy, world_audit, world_determinism, determinism_harness, resource_chain, construction, market_*, ai_skill_harness, order_book, build_spree, corp_ai, chain_depth and player_seed_sweep all pass. ai_skill_harness's bands HELD - no bless needed. spectator_determinism's byte-identity golden re-blessed with the reason recorded.

items.title: A mine now yields a basket and every UI surface still shows one resource - and one of them multiplies the basket by the wrong price
items.summary: BL-437 made an extraction site work every deposit on its tile, but every UI surface still reads only building_component::target_resource - entity_summary's 'Target:', hover_content's 'Extracting:', the corporation dashboard and the selection panel all name one resource for a building that now produces several. Worse, body_surface_canvas.cpp:1239 values a site as output_quantity x price[target_resource]: since BL-437 output_quantity is the WHOLE BASKET while the price is the primary's, so the on-canvas value figure is now arithmetically wrong whenever a tile carries more than one deposit.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 during the Sprint 19 playtest, from reading the surfaces rather than
from playing them - the gap is unambiguous in the code.

## Two problems, one cause

BL-437 changed what an extraction site DOES without changing what any surface SAYS.

1. **Presentation.** Four surfaces name exactly one resource for a site that now
   produces a basket: `entity_summary.cpp:173` ("Target: %s"), `hover_content.cpp:116`
   ("Extracting: %s"), `corporation_dashboard.cpp:28`, `selection_panel.cpp:1543`.
   A player watching coal accumulate with no building anywhere claiming to mine coal
   has no way to understand their own economy.

2. **A REAL ARITHMETIC BUG**, and it is the urgent half. `body_surface_canvas.cpp:1239`:
       value = br.output_quantity * price[br.target_resource]
   `output_quantity` is the sum over every deposit worked (economy_system.cpp's
   co-extraction block sets it to `produced_total`), while the price is the PRIMARY's.
   On a tile whose secondary deposits are worth more or less than its primary, this
   figure is simply wrong, and it was correct before BL-437.

## What it needs

`building_report` carries one `target_resource` and one total, so the per-resource
breakdown is not currently recoverable by any reader - the same limitation that made
tier_margin misreport coal as unmined (it had to switch to measuring reserve depletion
instead). The honest fix is for the report to carry the basket, which then serves the
valuation AND every presentation surface from one source.

Smaller alternative if that is too heavy: value the site by summing over the tile's
deposits at their own prices, and have the surfaces render the tile's worked deposits
rather than the stored primary. That fixes the output without touching the report, at
the cost of each reader re-deriving the split.

## Note

The presentation half is BL-437's own follow-on and was foreseeable when it landed;
the valuation bug was not noticed and is a genuine regression introduced by it.

items.title: The AI build scorer cannot build a processing facility - it enumerates extraction sites and one military base, and nothing else, so no rival can ever climb the production chain
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17 while verifying BL-417 (AI build score is quadratic). corp_ai.cpp emits corp_verb::build from exactly two places: the ranked_sites loop, hard-coded to building_type::extraction_site, and the single military_base candidate. There is no processing_facility build candidate anywhere in the scorer. The seam is fine - corp_command.cpp handles a build command naming a processor, recipe and all (BL-388), so a player or an MCP agent can build one; the deterministic scorer simply never asks. A rival corp therefore only ever owns the processors it was GENERATED with, for the whole campaign.
items.design:
Add a processing_facility build candidate to run_corp_strategic_step's enumeration, scored on the same curve as the extraction candidate and subject to the same solvency, glut and reserve-floor gates. Three things the extraction candidate does not have to solve, and this one does: (a) SITING - a processor is not sited by a deposit, so the ranked_sites list gives no candidate tiles; it needs its own siting rule (near the corp's own input supply / near a market / within logistics reach of both). (b) RECIPE CHOICE - the command must name one (corp_command rejects a recipe that does not match the type, and construct_building silently substitutes steel for no_recipe, which is exactly the trap BL-388 closed); recipe_margin already exists in this file and is the natural scorer. (c) INPUT ACCESS - a processor with no reachable input is an immediate loss-maker, and the BL-203 should-have buffer already prices feeding running processors, so the candidate must be gated on the corp being able to source its recipe's inputs at all.

This is NOT a tuning change and must not be folded into one. It changes which buildings exist in every evolved world, so it reshuffles every blessed golden and every ai_skill_harness band - that reshuffle is the item's cost, paid once, deliberately, and re-blessed as part of landing it. Guard: extend ai_skill_harness with an assertion that at least one rival corp builds at least one processing_facility over the run, which today would fail by construction.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): HELD on task C only (golden re-bless, Ben's NR-269 pick). A/B/D landed at debfa87 — corp_ai.cpp:736-905 processing candidate + ai_skill_harness guard; req R6 failed = the bands FELL and blessing would record bankruptcy as expected. Sequencing insight from the audit: BL-443's interest finding (98.8% of deficit) means landing the debt lever first may make C's bands legible without tuning. Order: BL-443 → re-run → C.
items.consequences_for_shipped_claims:
Three shipped claims are wrong because of this, corrected 2026-08-17 (see NR-265, NR-266, NR-267):

1. BL-436's design says corp_ai's build scorer 'is being asked to prefer processors on a payback curve that does not reward them'. It is not being asked anything of the sort - processors are not candidates. 'The AI prefers mines' is STRUCTURAL, not a scoring-curve artefact. This reassigns the blame BL-417 was filed to test: BL-417's quadratic curve is real and worth writing out honestly, but it was never the reason rivals do not build processors.

2. BL-436's calibration_sweep narrative explains the x4 collapse as corps 'spending the extra income building processors that lose MORE per tick at higher scale'. That mechanism is impossible - the AI cannot build a processor. Whatever the sweep measured, it was generated and warm-start processors only, and the conclusion needs re-deriving before any cost-side number moves. Do NOT re-tune on the old narrative.

3. BL-428 (chain depth) gates recipes on a corp's reached depth. A rival that cannot build a processor can never increase its depth, so the growth gate has no AI player. Ancient-only today, so it does not bite a 1960 campaign - but the ladder is currently single-player by construction.

items.title: An extraction site can only target the RICHEST resource on its tile, so a resource that is never the richest anywhere is never mined — coal has 1,671 tiles, 0 mines, and binds 54% of all starved processor ticks
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17, chasing why processing starves after BL-436 enabled the richness conversion and BL-439 fixed the no-recipe defect. Both the AI scorer (rank_extraction_sites) and world generation (author_building) pick an extraction target with placement_rules::richest_extractable(tile) — the single richest extractable deposit on that tile. A resource that is present on many tiles but rarely the richest on ANY of them is therefore structurally unmineable, whatever the demand for it. Coal is the worked example: 1,671 tiles carry it, it is the richest extractable on 1.1% of them, ZERO extraction sites target it, and it is the binding input on 54.0% of all starved processing building-ticks. The same shape appears in tier_margin R5 for resource ids 8/9/10, flagged as siting/reach by NR-266.
items.design:
The rule is a TILE-LOCAL heuristic making a decision that needs a WORLD-level fact. Richness answers "what is most abundant here"; siting needs "what is worth extracting here", and those differ exactly when a wanted good is common-but-never-dominant. Three parts, in order:

(a) ENUMERATE, do not pre-select. rank_extraction_sites emits at most one candidate per tile, at the richest target, so no scorer can ever see the alternative. It should emit a candidate per extractable target the tile carries (bounded by the existing top_m_sites cut), and let the existing net/glut/solvency scoring choose. This alone does not fix coal — coal loses on richness and would still be out-scored — but without it there is nothing for (b) to act on.

(b) LET UNMET INPUT DEMAND WEIGH. A resource that a loaded recipe names as an input and that nothing produces is a world fact, derivable deterministically from the registry plus current production, and it is exactly what tier_margin R4 already computes. Weight a candidate target by that shortfall. This is NOT a price signal and must not be routed through one: the price signal cannot work here by construction, because a processor has to be RUNNING to bid for coal, and it cannot run without coal. The deadlock is the defect.

(c) GENERATION uses the same rule, so a fresh world should not open with the shortage already baked in (author_building calls richest_extractable directly). Fix both or the AI spends the campaign digging out of a hole generation made.

Deliberately NOT in scope: repricing (NR-271), processing upkeep, and the richness band. Calibrating any of them against a chain whose second input is unobtainable would tune around the shortage and have to be undone once it is mined.

Guard: extend tier_margin R5 from a report into an assertion — no resource that a loaded recipe names as an input may have deposits on more than a threshold number of tiles and zero sites targeting it. That row fails today on coal by construction, and on ids 8/9/10 besides, so it must be run against the pre-change build first to prove it discriminates.

PROGRESS 2026-08-17. (a) and (b) are BUILT: rank_extraction_sites now emits a candidate per extractable deposit on a tile instead of one for its richest, weighted by input_demand_weights() — recipes-wanting-it over sites-already-named-for-it, so the pull is self-limiting and decays as the shortage is answered. corp_ai_params::input_demand_pull (default 4.0) makes it a data change; 0 restores the old behaviour.

(c) IS THE HALF THAT MOVES THE NUMBERS, and it is not done. tier_margin is BYTE-IDENTICAL across (a)+(b) — extraction 14.53/7.82, processing 12.37/-10.44, samples 2993/1916, and all seven UNSITEABLE rows still red. A 3-seed 20-tick run is dominated by GENERATED assets, and generation still sites by richest_extractable in author_building. The AI fix cannot show until generation stops digging the hole.

The blocker on (c) is structural and is the same one assign_default_recipes has: generate_corporations runs inside make_hard_coded_world, BEFORE the Lua economy layer loads, so it cannot see recipe demand any more than it can see recipe ids. Two shapes, and this is a DESIGN CALL rather than an implementation detail:
  (i) a post-registry retarget pass — a sibling of assign_default_recipes that walks generated extraction sites and re-points a site whose tile also carries a starved input. Cheap, consistent with the pattern already established, and needs no generation restructuring. It mutates a generated decision after the fact, which is only defensible because BL-437 made a site work its whole tile, so target_resource names what a site is FOR rather than all it extracts.
  (ii) hand generation a static demand hint so it sites correctly first time. Cleaner in principle, and it means the opening world is right rather than corrected, but it needs the recipe graph available at world-gen time, which is the ordering constraint the whole file is built around.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): HELD — 2/4. (a)+(b) landed (97fe33a: input_demand_weights/rank_extraction_sites, corp_ai.cpp:434-593); (c) SUPERSEDED by BL-441/BL-442 (both complete, 8cc2981) — do not build; (d) PRODUCTION.md propagation not started. Owed measurement first: re-run tier_margin R4b now that BL-441/442 are in — green means only (d) remains; red re-opens (c) in a new shape (NR-354 option A).
items.consequences_for_shipped_claims: It reassigns BL-436 one more time, and this is the third reassignment in two days. BL-436 was filed as "processing underearns extraction", diagnosed as a scoring-curve artefact (wrong — NR-265, it was structural), then as a richness rate ratio (right, and fixed by enabling richness_reference at the median), and now the residual is neither margin nor upkeep but SUPPLY: 46.3% of processing building-ticks starve, and over half of that is one resource nobody can mine. NR-271s sized price options (a/b/c) were all measured on a starved chain and must be re-derived after this lands, not applied before it.

items.title: The market demand register records FILLS, not WANTS — a starved processor that wanted 16 coal and got 2 registers demand of 2, so scarcity is invisible to the price signal
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17 testing Ben's proposal to widen the price band. market_clearing.cpp:601 reads `w.markets.at(mid).demand[r] += qty` where qty is bought[r] — what a corp ACTUALLY BOUGHT. A processor that needed 16 units of an input and could only draw 2 registers demand of 2. The resource therefore reads to resolve_price as one almost nobody wants, its price never rises, and no band width can amplify a signal that is zero. resolve_price ALREADY does the right thing given real numbers — its own line 34 comment reads "demand with no supply — top of the band" — so the pricing mechanism is built and correct; it is being starved of input.
items.design:
Register the WANT alongside the FILL. run_processing already computes the full-run need per input before deciding coverage (economy_system.cpp, the BL-130 pool + inventory coverage loop) — that figure is the demand, and it is already in hand at exactly the point the shortfall is known. It must reach mc.demand whether or not the draw succeeded.

Two things to keep straight, because conflating them is how this defect reads as correct: SUPPLY is an offer and INVENTORY is a delivery (the distinction BL-422 landed and MARKETS.md records). Demand needs the same split — what was WANTED versus what was BOUGHT. The purchase record (auto_buys, the VWAP accumulator, the money actually paid) must keep reading the FILL; only the price-resolution input changes to the want. Paying for goods nobody delivered would be BL-422 s defect in the opposite direction.

Determinism: the want must be accumulated in a deterministic order — this is the same seam where BL-422 found a latent unordered_map float-accumulation nondeterminism, so accumulate over a sorted key set, not a hash order.

GUARD, and it must be shown to fail on the pre-change build: a processor starved of an input registers demand equal to its full-run NEED, not to the quantity it managed to draw; and a resource with real demand and no supply resolves to the top of the price band rather than to base.
items.consequences_for_shipped_claims:
It corrects a claim this session made twice, including in BL-440 s own design: that the price signal "cannot work here by construction, because a processor must be RUNNING to bid a scarce input s price up and cannot run without it". The deadlock is real but it is not structural — it exists only because the register records fills. Once it records wants, price CAN do the siting work, and BL-440 (a)+(b) s per-deposit enumeration is what lets the scorer act on it. BL-440 (c) — a static demand hint handed to world generation — is SUPERSEDED and should not be built: it works around a cause this item removes.

## CLOSED 2026-08-19
Found already landed on `main` when this item was picked up for delivery — the fix shipped 2026-08-17 in commit 37989d1 ("A processor that could not buy what it needed said nothing (BL-441)"), merged at f0a50ce. mc.demand now accumulates from `report.wants` (a std::map, sorted-key accumulation per the determinism note above), with `report.purchases` kept strictly as the money/fill side. Guard lives in tools/verify/order_book_harness.cpp; the commit's own report records the guard failing pre-change (starved demand=0.000, price stuck at base) and passing post-change (demand=8.000, price=12.500). Only backlog.json's status was stale — flipped to complete here, no code change made this session. Worktree: worktree-agent-aa88fbeaf8cfec049.

items.title: The price band is hard-coded as constexpr in TWO places and is far too narrow for scarcity to cross an inter-market margin
items.summary: The [0.25x, 4x] price band lives as constexpr floats in market_clearing.cpp AND again in economy_system.cpp:399-400, the second carrying the comment "mirror market_clearing.cpp price band" — a duplication kept in step by hand. It is not in economy.lua, so the single most load-bearing economic tunable in the game is a code change rather than a data one, in two files that can silently diverge.
items.design:
TWO STEPS, and the first must land BEHAVIOUR-IDENTICAL. (1) Move the band to scripts/economy.lua as ONE authored pair, read through recipe_registry like every other tunable, with both call sites reading the same value. Verify byte-identical output across the move before touching the numbers — a refactor and a re-tune in one commit is how a golden move becomes unattributable. Add a guard that the two sites cannot diverge again.

(2) WIDEN, but only against measurement, and only after BL-441 lands. Ben s target (2026-08-17) is that scarcity must price high enough to CROSS THE MARGIN FOR NEARBY MARKETS, so inter-market trading exists from day 1 rather than as a late-game unlock. That makes the ceiling a function of the transport cost between adjacent markets, not a round number: the widened ceiling has to exceed base + haulage for a neighbouring market to be worth serving. Derive it from the logistics cost the supply layer already charges, and state the derivation in MARKETS.md.

Today s ceiling is why nothing moves: coal s base is 2.0, so its scarcity ceiling is 8.0 against iron ore s 10.0 — a resource nobody can obtain is still cheaper than the one everybody has.

BLOCKED ON BL-441 for step 2 only. Widening a band whose demand input is structurally zero amplifies nothing; step 1 can run immediately.

## CLOSED 2026-08-19
This item was picked up for delivery scoped to step 1 only (this session's instructions were explicit: do not widen the band, leave status as designed, note step 2 as remaining). On inspection, BOTH steps were already landed on `main` from the 2026-08-17 session: step 1 in commit 9fb90e2 ("The price band was written down twice and synchronised by hand"), merged at 5e442d1 onto BL-441; step 2 in commit 2a7aa01 ("The scarcity ceiling is now derived from measured haulage, not authored"), which moved economy.price_band.ceil_mult from 4.0 to 10.0, DERIVED from tools/verify/haulage_measure.cpp's measured per-unit haulage cost (median 0.70, p90 1.67, max 4.83 over 5 seeds) rather than picked — satisfying this item's own step-2 requirement that the ceiling be measured, not authored. Step 1's guard (tools/verify/price_band_harness.cpp) is differential and includes a negative control (reintroducing a local 0.25f/4.0f constant fails). Step 1 was independently verified behaviour-identical in its own commit message (order_book_harness, econ_harness, spectator_determinism byte-identical; econ_stability byte-identical apart from wall-clock lines). Given step 2 already landed with its own proper derivation and sign-off trail, flipping this item's status to complete rather than leaving it artificially open — see NEEDS_REVIEW.json for the judgment call. Worktree: worktree-agent-aa88fbeaf8cfec049.

items.title: A corp that dips one quarter into the red compounds at 2%/tick forever, so a few thousand of operating loss reads as millions and every economy measurement downstream becomes unreadable
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17 while reading ai_skill_harness's -2M to -3.4M net worths (NR-269). k_debt_interest_per_quarter is 0.02 and the benchmark rollout is 300 ticks: 1.02^300 = 380x. Per-building extraction nets +5 to +11 on every seed, so a corp cannot lose millions by operating. It dips a few thousand negative on processor upkeep and compounding does the rest. The rate itself is defensible (~8%/yr); what is missing is any floor, recovery path or terminal state. An insolvent corp is not resolved, it just accelerates away from zero.
items.design:
MEASURE BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING, and the measurement is the first deliverable: decompose a benchmark corp's final balance into operating flows versus accrued interest. The claim that the -3M is 'almost entirely compounding' is arithmetic inference from 1.02^300, not an observation, and it should be confirmed or overturned before a lever is chosen.

Note tools/verify/econ_bankruptcy.cpp ALREADY EXISTS and budget_system.hpp names it as a reader of the interest constant, yet budget_system.cpp contains no bankruptcy handling at all. Read that harness first: it may already pin the spiral as expected behaviour, in which case this item is partly a disagreement with an existing check rather than a new defect, and that has to be settled openly rather than by editing the check.

The design question is what insolvency MEANS, and it is a game-design call, not an arithmetic one. Candidates, deliberately not chosen here: (a) a debt ceiling past which no further interest accrues, cheapest and least meaningful; (b) forced liquidation - assets sold to clear debt, which gives 'survival' a real definition and makes the survival metric mean something it currently does not; (c) restructuring, where a corp idles or sheds buildings to return to solvency, which is the version that composes with the existing BL-079 reflex tier and the BL-202 scorer rather than sitting beside them.

(b) and (c) are the ones that feed Conflict and Trade; (a) only silences a number. Prefer whichever the measurement supports, and state the reason.

GUARD: a corp driven insolvent reaches a defined terminal or recovered state within a bounded number of ticks, rather than diverging. Must be shown to fail pre-change - today it diverges by construction.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19: Re-homed v0.1.16 -> v0.1.11: rides Lane D's first batch as its cheapest economy-truth unblock (Fall-arc amendment 5: interest is 98.8% of every benchmark deficit). Verify build state first — N1 lists this among the seven unaudited Sprint-26 items.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): CONFIRMED genuinely unbuilt by the N1 audit — the only code is the 2% charge itself (budget_system.cpp:218-226); zero floor/cap/reserve/terminal code in src/. Measurement phase landed (0a79c4c, debt_decomposition.cpp): interest = 98.7–98.8% of deficit on all five seeds. TWO GATES before building, both Ben's (NR-296): (1) which lever — the measurement argues against a ceiling (censors the variable) and against liquidation (base_capital defaults 0.0, everyone liquidates by tick 30), recommends (c) restructuring via BL-079's reflex tier gated on solvency; (2) is a corp opening at balance 0 intended with no warm start? ALSO: collides with BL-480 on budget_system.cpp — build only after MB merges. NR-297: debt_decomposition should grow this item's real assertion and be registered as a guard (skill registration = Ben's permission).
items.consequences_for_shipped_claims: It puts a question mark over ai_skill_harness's net-worth bands as a SKILL signal at all. If final net worth is dominated by compounding on an early dip, the metric is measuring how early a corp first went negative, not how well it played - and the bands have been blessed and re-blessed against that number repeatedly. The survival fraction may be the sounder signal; it is currently the one metric that has stayed green throughout Sprint 19.

items.title: No check asserts that a corp_verb is reachable from all three directions
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. The seam has 15 verbs. The dictionary covers 15, a UI press covers 12, the rival scorer emits 8. Nothing measures that, so the gap was found by hand and will go stale by hand. WIDENED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-308): the tool also carries an authored subsystem column, so a subsystem owning no verb at all is visible rather than inferred - the convoy layer being the case that proves it. Reported, never failed; difficulty 2 -> 3.
items.design:
## What the audit measured

Three artefacts already carry the answer, and no tool joins them.

- `src/world/corp_command.hpp` is the authoritative verb list (15, append-only).
- `docs/ai/ACTIONS.json` gameplay family transcribes it (15 entries, complete today).
- Each dictionary entry carries a `surface` field naming its UI press, or saying SEAM-ONLY.
- `src/world/corp_ai.cpp` assigns `cmd.verb` at exactly ten sites, covering eight distinct verbs.

The join is mechanical and cheap. It is not written.

## Shape

A node tool, `tools/session/verb_coverage.js`, emitting one row per verb with four columns:
seam / dictionary / UI press / AI candidate. Sources, in order of authority:

1. Parse the `corp_verb` enum out of `corp_command.hpp` — the seam wins over everything.
2. Read `ACTIONS.json` gameplay entries; a missing verb is a dictionary defect, and per
   BL-270 the dictionary is the wrong one when they disagree.
3. Read each entry `surface` field; a `SEAM-ONLY` marker means no human press. This is the
   one axis read from prose rather than code, and it is deliberate — the prose is the
   maintained record, and a grep of `src/ui` for a verb name finds nothing useful because
   the UI calls seam functions, not verbs.
4. Grep `corp_ai.cpp` for `cmd.verb = corp_verb::X` assignments.

Exit non-zero on a **dictionary** gap only. UI and AI gaps are reported, not failed — they
are legitimate design states (`set_workforce_auto` may well be correctly AI-absent), and a
tool that fails on them would be muted within a week.

## Why it is priority A for its size

It is the instrument the reachability argument rests on. Sprint 22 proposes closing gaps;
without this the closing is unverified and the reopening is unnoticed. Per CLAUDE.md
§ Tool creation is skill creation, it should be wrapped or invoked from an existing skill
rather than left loose.

## WIDENED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-308): add a subsystem column

The four-column join above answers *"is each verb that exists reachable"*. It cannot answer
*"does each subsystem own a verb at all"*, because a join over existing verbs is structurally
blind to the absent one. The Sprint 25 audit found the gap that proves it: the convoy layer —
`supply_system.cpp` plus the whole of `logistics.cpp` plus four rendering paths, and the
only coupling between two markets' prices — owns **zero** of the fifteen verbs, and this
tool as first scoped would have reported a clean sheet over it.

**Shape.** A second table: one row per world subsystem, listing the verbs whose subject
belongs to it and a count. The subsystem list is **authored, not derived** — a hand-kept
list in the tool naming each `src/world` subsystem and its verbs, reviewed when a
subsystem is added. Deriving it from filenames would be clever and wrong: it would silently
grow a row for every new file and mean nothing.

**Reported, never failed.** A subsystem legitimately owning no verb is a real design state —
`market_clearing` should not take player commands. The row exists so the absence is
*visible and deliberate* rather than inferred, which is the same reasoning BL-451 uses for
printing a per-verb histogram it never asserts on.

**Difficulty 2 → 3.** Still small, but it is a second data source and a maintained list.

LANDED 2026-08-19 (Batch Delivery). Built tools/session/verb_coverage.js: Table 1 joins corp_command.hpp's 24-verb seam, ACTIONS.json's dictionary, each entry's surface field (UI press), and corp_ai.cpp's grep-derived AI-candidate set; exits non-zero only on a dictionary gap. Table 2 is an authored per-subsystem verb-ownership map, reported never failed. First real run found a genuine dictionary gap - march_unit/halt_unit/disband_unit (BL-470, appended 2026-08-19) are missing from ACTIONS.json, exit code 1 - logged as NR-373, left open as a follow-up (not this item's scope to close).

items.title: Three procurement verbs are reachable by an agent and by no human
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. request_quote, accept_quote and cancel_contract landed with world state, serialisation and a harness, and no press. The dictionary already records all three as SEAM-ONLY in as many words.
items.design:
## The gap, in the dictionary own words

All three entries open identically: *No UI. SEAM-ONLY: this verb has NO player-facing
press.* BL-350 (procurement seam) landed the state, the serialisation and the harness and
stopped short of the surface. So an external agent can contract for goods and a human
cannot — the exact asymmetry the reachability argument exists to catch, and the largest
one on the board.

## Shape

A **Contracts** tab on the Market Ledger, beside Sell Orders, scoped to the ledger
selected body the way Sell Orders already is. Three regions:

- **Request** — supplier combo, resource combo, quantity, a Request button. The four
  decline results (`rejected_no_capacity`, `no_input_access`, `embargo`, `reputation`)
  are already distinguishable at the seam, so each gets its own message rather than a
  generic failure. That distinguishability was designed in and is currently unread by
  anything.
- **Live quotes** — one row per quote with price, lead time, deposit, and Accept.
- **Contracts in flight** — progress, remaining, and Cancel behind a confirm popup
  (irreversible and forfeits the deposit, so it follows the demolish precedent).

## What it must not do

It must not add a fourth code path. The presses issue `corp_command` records through
`apply_corp_command`, exactly as the Sell Orders tab does since BL-293, so the human and
the agent share one seam and one validation.

## Owed alongside

A `question_log.json` entry per region (the pair is required on every surface), and the
three `ACTIONS.json` entries rewritten — their `surface` and `press` fields currently
assert there is no UI, which is precisely the kind of stale entry BL-270 warns misleads
the AI player.

items.title: The rival scorer enumerates no procurement candidate
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. corp_ai.cpp assigns cmd.verb at ten sites and none of them is request_quote, accept_quote or cancel_contract. BL-350 gave rivals a procurement seam they never use.
items.design:
## The gap

BL-293 (order book on the seam) gave rivals the sell side. The buy side arrived with
BL-350 (procurement seam) and no scorer touched it. A rival whose local market cannot
supply a recipe input has exactly one remedy today — build differently — when the seam
offers a second.

## Shape, respecting the standing rules

One more candidate family on the existing deterministic scored-utility layer. No planner,
no new code path, legal verbs only:

- **Request.** For each completed building whose recipe is input-starved at its local
  market, score a `request_quote` against the highest-reputation supplier holding capacity.
  The supplier walk must be over a **sorted** corp id list — `w.corporations` is an
  unordered_map and iterating it directly is the nondeterminism BL-422 already caught once.
- **Accept.** Score each live quote against the counterfactual of buying the same goods on
  the open market over the lead time. Accept when the contract is cheaper *and* the
  deposit clears the solvency floor — the deposit is a spend and is subject to the reserve
  gate like every other, per the standing-rules ruling on NR-218.
- **Cancel.** Score only when the contracted good has become cheaper than the contract by
  more than the forfeited deposit. Deliberately conservative: cancellation moves
  reputation, and a scorer that churns contracts makes the reputation axis meaningless.

## Cap

One procurement command per evaluation, as `hire_unit` is capped. Contracts are durative
and a rival that opens six in a tick has committed cash it cannot see.

items.title: Three verbs the docs say the scorer uses, it does not emit
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. The standing rules describe rivals scoring "build, demolish, survey and road decisions each tick". The scorer emits build, survey, the four dials and place_sell_order. Demolish, place_road and remove_sell_order have no candidate site.
items.design:
## The discrepancy

`.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md` states the BL-202/BL-203 exception as *"build,
demolish, survey and road decisions scored each tick"*. Grepping `cmd.verb = corp_verb::`
in `corp_ai.cpp` returns ten sites covering eight verbs: build (x3), resume, idle,
set_workforce, set_recipe, survey, hire_unit, place_sell_order.

**Demolish and place_road are described and absent.** This is the backlog-prose-goes-stale
pattern applied to a standing rule, which is worse, because the rule is read as an
invariant rather than as a plan.

## Three separate calls, not one

1. **`demolish`** — a real gap. A rival with a persistently loss-making asset can idle it
   (and does) but never reclaims the tile. Idle is free and reversible, so the honest
   trigger is not "loss-making" but "the tile is worth more under a different building
   than this one is worth idled". That is a comparison against the build enumeration that
   already runs, so the candidate is cheap to site and easy to get wrong.
2. **`place_road`** — a real gap, and the one with a measurable payoff, since haulage is
   now instrumented (`haulage_measure`). Score a tier against the freight it would
   actually carry rather than against adjacency.
3. **`remove_sell_order`** — a real gap and the smallest. BL-293 gave rivals order
   placement and no withdrawal, so a floor priced for last quarter stands forever, and
   `max_sell_orders_per_corp` becomes a ceiling a long game will reach.

**`set_workforce_auto` is NOT in scope and is judged correctly absent.** It hands a dial
to an auto-solver; a scorer that already sets the dial has no use for it. Recorded so the
next audit does not re-file it.

## The doc half

Whichever of the three land, the standing-rules sentence and AI_OPPONENT.md are corrected
to the verbs actually emitted — and if one is deliberately not built, it is named as
deliberate rather than left reading as shipped.

items.title: No corp may be at war with, or allied to, another
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 on Ben's ruling the same date: hostility is a declared war state corps opt into deliberately, with a friend state alongside it - three modes (friend / neutral / hostile) as the substrate for naive diplomacy. Answers the risk Sprint 21 named and left unfiled. SETTLED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-302): the HYBRID reading - hostility stored directed, friendship stored symmetric, two tables with two key rules. Difficulty raised 4 -> 5: it is the most expensive of the three options and carries three non-optional invariants (a pending offer is not a stance; declaring hostility dissolves a friendship row atomically; consumers must not collapse the two tables behind one accessor). [COMPLETE 2026-08-19: src/world/stance.{hpp,cpp} landed — directed corp_hostile_pairs, symmetric corp_friend_pairs, pending corp_friend_offers; four corp_command verbs (declare_hostile, offer_friendship, accept_friendship, return_to_neutral); stance_determinism.cpp 36/36 PASS, in-memory replay only (no serialiser exists — see NR-349). Substrate landed inert per design, no consequence wired yet.]
items.design:
## Why now

The Sprint 21 proposal audit found that *"the capability everyone assumes exists and does
not is a hostility model"*, and flagged it as a design call filed as work nowhere. Ben
settled the design on 2026-08-17. This is that call, written as an item.

Without it there is no legal predicate on an attack verb, no engagement trigger condition,
and no way for the scorer to price an engagement. It blocks BL-315 (armed house conflict
spine) F2 entirely.

## Naming — do not call it standing

`src/world/standing.{hpp,cpp}` already exists and means something else: the BL-262 coarse
**power** read (negligible / minor / notable / major / dominant) over reach, capital and
market share. Overloading the word would make every future sentence about "a corp
standing" ambiguous between how strong it is and how it feels about you.

Proposed term: **stance**. `corp_stance { friendly, neutral, hostile }`, in
`src/world/stance.{hpp,cpp}`. GLOSSARY.md gets both terms with the distinction stated.

## The substrate that already exists

`world::corp_reputation` is a `std::map<std::pair<entity_id, entity_id>, float>` — already
directed, already serialised, already sorted-key deterministic. A stance table is the same
shape with an enum payload, so the data-model cost is near zero **if stance is directed**.
See the symmetry question below, which is exactly the question of whether it may be.

`condition_set` and `rejected_embargo` also already exist: `request_quote` declines when a
supplier condition set evaluates false against the buyer. So there is already a
relationship-shaped gate in the economy, and stance should feed it rather than sit beside it.

## SETTLED 2026-08-17 (Ben, on NR-302): HYBRID — hostility directed, friendship symmetric

The question was directed (A), symmetric (B), or hybrid. **Ben chose the hybrid**, and the
recommendation on file was A — so this is a deliberate overrule and the reason matters:
the hybrid is the only reading that is honest to *both* halves of the fiction at once.
**You can be attacked without agreeing. You cannot be befriended without agreeing.** A and
B each get one half of that right and the other half wrong.

### What it costs, stated plainly, because this is the most expensive of the three

**Two tables with two different key rules**, and that is the whole of the added cost:

| | Hostility | Friendship |
|---|---|---|
| Key | directed `(actor, target)` | canonicalised `(min id, max id)` |
| Shape | `std::map<std::pair<entity_id,entity_id>, bool>` — same as `corp_reputation` | one row per pair |
| Verb | `declare_hostile` — unilateral, immediate | `offer_friendship` → `accept_friendship` |
| Undo | `return_to_neutral`, unilateral | `return_to_neutral`, unilateral **by either party** |
| One-sided state? | **yes, and it is the point** — an ambush | **impossible by construction** |

### The three invariants this shape needs, and none of them are optional

1. **A pending offer is not a stance.** It lives in its own store, not in the friendship
   table, or an unaccepted offer reads as a friendship to every consumer. Accepting moves
   it; declining or expiring erases it.
2. **Hostility outranks friendship when both exist.** The hybrid makes this reachable —
   A and B are friends (symmetric row) and then A declares hostile (directed row). The
   resolution rule is that **declaring hostility dissolves the friendship row atomically**,
   in the same command, rather than leaving a contradictory pair for consumers to
   arbitrate. A rejected declaration mutates neither table.
3. **Consumers must ask the right question of the right table.** `is_hostile(a, b)` is
   directional and `are_friends(a, b)` is not, and the two must not be collapsed behind a
   single `stance_between()` accessor that hides which is which. That convenience is the
   most likely way this design gets silently flattened back to B.

### What it buys, which is why it is worth the second table

The ambush survives — BL-458 (interdiction) can intercept a convoy belonging to a corp that
does not yet know it is at war, which is the single most characteristic thing a hostile act
can be. And friendship keeps the property that makes it meaningful: it cannot be imposed,
so a friendly row is always evidence that two corps both chose it.

## Scope

World state, the three verbs (`declare_hostile`, `offer_friendship`, `accept_friendship`,
plus a return-to-neutral), serialisation, and a determinism harness. **No consequence** —
stance gates nothing in this item. What hostility permits is BL-315 (armed house conflict
spine); what friendship permits is a later call. Landing the substrate inert is deliberate:
it lets the model be argued about against a real save rather than against prose.

items.design:
## Why a separate item

BL-350 (procurement seam) landed a complete seam with no press, and nobody noticed for
